title: Impending Engine Failure and PEL
summary: Recognizing engine trouble early and using the precautionary emergency landing profile before it becomes a forced landing.
overview: This event teaches how to identify an engine that may be failing before total power loss occurs. You will practice spotting warning signs, deciding when a PEL is warranted, flying the emergency landing pattern early, and using DEGA and PEL(P) concepts to preserve enough energy and runway options before the situation becomes a forced landing or ejection scenario.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items
studyNotes.summary: The event is about acting early. If engine reliability is in doubt, get the airplane pointed at a runway and fly the PEL profile before the problem takes that option away.

items.text: Engine failure may arrive with little warning, but several signs point to a degrading engine before total power loss.

children.text: Excessive vibration, smoke, fumes, or unusual engine noise.
CHIP annunciation, oil-pressure problems, low fuel pressure, or high fuel flow.
Uncommanded power changes, loss of power, uncommanded propeller feather, or compressor stalls.

items.text: If any condition makes engine reliability doubtful, plan for a PEL immediately instead of waiting for a confirmed failure.
A PEL is used when engine failure is suspected or directed by checklist, but usable power still exists.

children.text: Turn toward the nearest suitable field.
Keep the aircraft clean until configuration changes are actually needed.
Use available power early to stay on profile.

items.text: Do not delay configuration changes to try to rescue a low-energy profile late. If power is available in a PEL, use it.
PEL(P) simulates the same problem from inside the landing pattern and trains you to intercept the ELP by or before Low Key.

children.text: Use boost pump and ignition only when an airstart would be appropriate.
Reduce power on the ELP, lower gear when appropriate, and complete the pattern with minimum 120 KIAS discipline.

items.text: High Key, Low Key, and DEGA calculations matter because they tell you whether a paved field remains reachable and whether you still have recovery options.
This event rewards early judgment more than troubleshooting depth.
If the engine worsens during the PEL, transition immediately to Engine Failure During Flight and then Forced Landing or Eject as required.
Do not lower landing flaps until landing is assured. Preserve glide distance until the runway is actually made.
